opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really useful way to frame things, because depth and breadth pull on different capabilities.

Depth is about how long and how complex a single task is. Writing one function is shallow; building and maintaining a whole software project over weeks is deep. As tasks get deeper, the agent needs to plan over long horizons, keep track of state, recover from its own mistakes, and know when something has gone wrong. That puts a lot of pressure on memory and context: how you carry information forward, what you summarize, what you forget. It also changes how you evaluate. With a short task you check the answer. With a long task the intermediate process matters, because one small error early can compound.

Breadth is about how many different kinds of tasks and environments an agent can handle. Coding, web browsing, using a computer, doing research, talking to customers. Each environment has its own interface, feedback signals, and notion of success. Breadth means the agent needs strong priors and general reasoning so it can generalize instead of being hand-engineered for each domain. That's where language models changed things: earlier reinforcement learning agents could go deep in one game but couldn't transfer at all, while language gives you a kind of universal prior that lets you go broad.

The interesting part is the interaction. Many valuable real-world tasks are deep and broad at the same time. Think of a human employee: over a month they switch between tools, talk to different people, and pursue goals that span many steps. To get there, I think we need progress on a few fronts. Better environments and benchmarks that actually reflect long-horizon, real-world work. Better memory, so agents can learn from experience over time instead of starting fresh each episode. And better ways to define reward when the outcome is fuzzy or delayed.

So my short answer: depth pushes you toward long-term memory, planning, and robustness; breadth pushes you toward generalization and good priors. The next phase of agents is about combining the two, and a lot of that comes down to choosing the right tasks and environments to work on, not just building bigger models.

r001.rationale: It says deeper tasks require agents to plan over long horizons and explicitly identifies better long-term memory as needed.

r002.rationale: It describes breadth as handling varied tasks and environments, but does not connect that breadth to multi-agent research.

fable-5.1.text:
I think depth and breadth are actually two quite different axes, and they pull on different capabilities.

Depth is about how long a horizon the agent has to reason over to get one thing right. If I ask an agent to solve a hard math problem, or debug a complex system, the task is narrow, but it requires many steps of reasoning, and errors compound. So what you need there is mostly strong reasoning, self-verification, the ability to backtrack. That's largely what reinforcement learning on reasoning has pushed on, and I think that's where we've seen the fastest progress, because the environments are relatively clean and the reward is relatively clear.

Breadth is the opposite. It's about how many different kinds of situations the agent has to handle, how messy and heterogeneous the world it operates in is. A real assistant has to deal with a browser one minute, a terminal the next, an email thread, a half-specified request from a person. Each individual step might be shallow, but the space of things it has to cope with is enormous. And breadth is where I think agents are still weak, because you can't get it from a single well-defined environment. You get it from exposure to a lot of diverse environments, from good priors that come out of language pretraining, and from the ability to generalize to tools and interfaces you haven't seen before.

So my view is that the agents that matter most will need both, and the interesting question is how they interact. A very deep reasoner that only works in a few environments is a tool. A very broad agent that can't think deeply is a toy. The research challenge is building environments and training signals where the agent has to be broad and deep at the same time, and I think that is the direction the field is moving, from benchmarks that test one isolated skill toward tasks that look like real work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses long reasoning horizons, but does not identify long-term memory as a requirement.

r002.rationale: It describes breadth as a challenge requiring diverse environments and generalization, but does not connect increasing breadth to multi-agent research.

astra-6.text:
I think depth and breadth put different demands on an agent. Depth is about how far it has to go to finish a task: how many steps it needs to take, whether it can recognize a mistake, and whether it can recover and keep making progress. Breadth is about how many different kinds of situations it needs to handle—different tools, environments, and goals.

For a deep task in a narrow domain, you can build quite a lot of structure around the model. You know what actions are available and what success looks like. But as you increase breadth, it becomes harder to anticipate every situation. The model has to decide which tools are relevant, what information it’s missing, and sometimes whether it should ask the user a question.

And these dimensions interact. Being able to do one step across many domains doesn’t necessarily mean you can complete a long task in any of them. Small errors accumulate, and an early misunderstanding can send the whole process in the wrong direction. So the challenge is to combine flexibility with reliable execution: not just knowing what to do next, but checking whether that action actually moved you toward the goal.

r001.rationale: The response discusses long, multi-step tasks and recovering from mistakes, but does not identify long-term memory as a requirement.

r002.rationale: It explains that broader tasks require flexibility across tools and situations, but does not connect increasing breadth to multi-agent research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think depth and breadth put different demands on an agent. Depth is about how far it has to go to finish a task: how many steps it needs, whether it can recognize mistakes, and whether it can recover and keep making progress. Even if each individual step is fairly reliable, a long sequence can still fail. So deeper tasks require planning, feedback, and some way to verify the result.

Breadth is about the range of situations the agent can handle. Can it work with different tools, adapt to a new environment, and figure out what information it needs? That requires generalization, but also judgment about when to ask a question or learn something before acting.

The two interact. An agent might handle many kinds of short tasks but struggle to complete one substantial project. Or it might do a very long workflow reliably in a narrow domain. So I would look at both: how broadly can it operate, and how deeply can it follow through? That also helps us understand whether the next improvement should come from the model, the tools, or the way we organize the agent’s interaction with its environment.

r001.rationale: The response discusses planning, feedback, and verification for deeper tasks, but does not identify long-term memory as a requirement.

r002.rationale: The response describes breadth as handling varied situations and tools, but does not connect increasing breadth to multi-agent research.
